parts.label: Understand
parts.title: Separate learning a task from generating an answer
parts.body:
Start with the decision the workflow needs. A supervised classifier learns from examples paired with target labels. It can fit a stable, narrow decision such as routing an invoice to a cost centre. A foundation model learns broad patterns during pretraining and can then be adapted to follow instructions. It handles varied language and drafts, but fluent output does not establish that an answer is supported or a business rule was applied correctly.

Deep learning describes layered representations; it is not a synonym for generative AI. Transformers use attention to relate tokens in context. At inference, a language model produces a continuation under supplied context and settings. Instruction tuning changes how it responds to requests; fine-tuning can adapt behaviour for a task. Neither gives it live access to current policy.

Separate four questions in a proposal: Is the task prediction, extraction, generation, or action? What data establishes a correct result? How costly is an error? How will the system obtain current, authorised information? A fixed rule or a conventional model may be easier to test when the task is stable. Compare options on the same cases.

example.title: An invoice routing choice
example.body: A shared service team has 12 invoice categories and labelled history. It tests rules, a classifier, and a general language model on unseen invoices, including blurred scans and new suppliers. Category-level accuracy, exception review, cost, and delay determine the choice.

exercise.title: Write the fit test
exercise.body: Choose one workflow. Classify the output as prediction, extraction, generation, or action. Describe a current-process baseline and two candidate methods. Specify representative held-out cases, severe errors, review effort, latency, and cost per accepted result. State who decides.

parts.label: Practice
parts.title: Read a model proposal without being impressed by its size
parts.body:
A foundation model can be reused across tasks, which makes experimentation easier. The proposal still needs to describe the actual system: model version, context, instructions, data access, output constraints, and review path. Parameter count or a public benchmark cannot tell you whether French customer complaints, Canadian tax forms, or unusual supplier invoices will work in your workflow. A benchmark reports performance on its own tasks and conditions.

Ask for a comparison against the existing process and a smaller viable option. Run each on the same held-out cases and report performance by task slice. Include human time spent preparing inputs and repairing outputs. Record where input data goes, vendor retention terms, and how a model-version change triggers fresh evaluation.

The selection memo should name the business owner, intended users, permitted data, minimum quality, failure severity, operating cost, fallback, and review date. Ask the technical lead to explain extra model complexity in terms of a measured gain on the task.

example.title: A benchmark that hides the wrong cases
example.body: A vendor reports 94% invoice classification accuracy. Finance finds 99% on recurring domestic suppliers and 61% on cross-border invoices. The team restricts the first release to domestic invoices while gathering better cross-border cases. Figures are illustrative.

exercise.title: Challenge the selection memo
exercise.body: Draft six questions for a team proposing a large model for a narrow workflow. Require a baseline, category-level results, error-cost analysis, data-handling terms, rollback trigger, and evidence that a simpler method falls short.

parts.label: Operate
parts.title: Understand the limits of context and multimodality
parts.body:
A text model works with tokens, without an unlimited view of every document. Longer prompts consume processing time and money, and the relevant material can still be missed among distracting content. Multimodal systems accept or produce images, audio, or other modalities, but each input type needs its own tests. A scanned document adds OCR or visual interpretation errors before the model reasons about its contents. Voice adds transcription, accent, and turn-taking failures.

For a document or image proposal, trace input capture, extraction, permission check, context assembly, model response, and human action. Give each stage an owner and a failure signal. Test poor scans, tables, rotated pages, regional formats, and languages actually used. A simple multilingual greeting is no evidence of task quality in another language.

Decide which uncertainties force abstention or human review. A system that cannot read an invoice number reliably should flag the field, preserve the image, and avoid posting a guessed amount. Show that uncertainty to the person who will act.

example.title: A document pipeline failure
example.body: A receipt assistant reads a faint '8' as '3' and produces a polished reimbursement summary. Field-level confidence and reconciliation against line items route it for review before the payment record changes.

exercise.title: Trace a multimodal case
exercise.body: Draw the stages for a scanned-document or voice workflow. At each stage name a failure, test case, consequence, and fallback. Include a relevant language or regional format.

parts.label: Apply
parts.title: Make the architecture decision explainable
parts.body:
Explain a model choice to a CFO and risk committee through the task, baseline, downside of error, and evidence from the case mix. A general model can fit varied language or drafting. A constrained method can fit a small set of stable labels. A combination may work: extraction proposes fields, rules check totals, and a person handles exceptions.

Write the decision boundary before a pilot. Specify outputs that can flow automatically, outputs needing sampling, and outputs requiring approval. Include configuration and test-set versions in the record. If the provider changes the model or the business starts using it for another task, earlier evidence may no longer support release.

Report value and burden in the same unit, such as cost per correctly completed case or accepted outcomes per hour. A fast answer that creates rework may slow the workflow. Keep a named owner, rollback trigger, and scheduled review after real use.

example.title: An invoice decision with the same case mix
example.body: On 1,000 held-out invoices (700 recurring, 200 cross-border, 100 poor scans), rules yield 870 accepted results, one severe misrouting, 230 review minutes, and $0.40 per accepted result. A classifier yields 925, one severe error, 160 minutes, and $0.55. A language model yields 948, seven severe errors, 180 minutes, and $1.20. The figures are illustrative and include human review in unit cost. The team chooses the classifier for recurring and cross-border categories, keeps poor scans in staff review, and withholds automatic posting. It can expand only after the severe errors are diagnosed and the poor-scan slice meets its own gate.

exercise.title: Write one decision record
exercise.body: Prepare a one-page record with task and baseline, two options, evaluation slices, controls, quality and cost results, selected scope, accountable owner, rollback trigger, and re-evaluation date. Mark invented figures as illustrative.
